Treat u>=0 as part of the meaning of unit roundoff; do not strengthen its smallness condition. Include n=0 if allowed and u=0. Preserve symmetry of Delta A and the componentwise interpretation of the bound.

In the latter case show its connection to the actual algorithm. Successful execution supplies valid square roots and nonzero divisors. Make explicit the standard rounded-square-root specification rhat=sqrt(s)*(1+delta), s>=0, |delta|<=u. The displayed common source model only lists +,-,*,/; the paper proof implicitly uses rounded sqrt. Justify sqrt semantics as part of floating-point Cholesky, rather than importing the desired error bound. If the approved interpretation permits only the four listed operations with no sqrt specification, record that precise missing semantic assumption as a blocker; those four-operation assumptions alone cannot constrain an arbitrary sqrt routine.

Prove positivity of 1+delta and bounds by gamma_m=m*u/(1-m*u) on products of at most m rounding factors and inverse factors, for m*u<1. Count repeated occurrences separately. Prove denominator positivity and monotonicity gamma_m<=gamma_(n+1) whenever m<=n+1. The opened generic memory supports establishing positive denominators explicitly before rational arithmetic; it supplies no mathematical result for this target.

Derive an exact sum of individually weighted real products for a sequential inner product of length l. Assign the first rounded product directly, then add subsequent rounded products; each coefficient has at most l factors. Cover empty and singleton sums separately. Cancellation forbids assuming a relative-error coefficient on the exact sum as a whole.

Derive a local perturbed scalar identity for each one-based i<j from the recorded dot product, subtraction, and division. Inner-product coefficients have at most i-1 factors; the pivot-product coefficient has two inverse rounding factors. For i>=2 their counts are <=n+1. Keep coefficient witnesses indexed by the particular entry and summand, without asserting one common perturbed factor matrix.

Prove the missing diagonal helper by squaring the rounded sqrt relation and solving the residual equation. For one-based j>=2 the pivot-square coefficient has one inverse subtraction factor and two inverse copies of the sqrt factor, hence three factors; dot-product coefficients have at most j-1. Both counts are <=j+1<=n+1. For j=1 use the direct rounded sqrt(A[1,1]) relation, requiring only two inverse factors. Bypass empty subtraction or prove its exactness in actual floating-point semantics; an unconstrained extra error on subtraction by zero would not justify the n=1 constant.

Construct Delta A = Rhat.transpose * Rhat - A. Connect its upper-half entries to the negative sum of local coefficient perturbations derived from the execution. Use finite-sum absolute-value bounds to obtain gamma_(n+1) times the sum of |Rhat[k,i]|*|Rhat[k,j]| for k<=min(i,j). The diagonal bound must contain squares |Rhat[k,j]|^2; the paper displays an unexplained primed factor there, which cannot be used as a hypothesis or propagated into the authoritative theorem.

Use triangularity to extend the restricted sums to all indices and identify them with (entrywiseAbs(Rhat.transpose)*entrywiseAbs(Rhat))[i,j]. Establish the exact equality Rhat.transpose*Rhat=A+Delta A from the construction. Do not replace the product of absolute-value matrices by absolute value of their product.
